rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads one lām and genitive al-ākhira as an annex; the others read two lāmāms and nominative al-ākhira as an adjective of dār. Annexation instead makes it describe the Hour.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر ولدار الآخرة بلام واحدة وجر الآخرة على الإضافة والباقون بلامين ورفع الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For أفلا تعقلون, some readers use second-person tāʾ, addressing the audience or letting direct address prevail; the others use third-person yāʾ, continuing the preceding reference to those who are mindful.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل المدينة وابن ذكوان عن ابن عامر ويعقوب وسهل أفلا تعقلون بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baght means sudden arrival; ḥasra is intense regret that exhausts the regretful; tafrīṭ means falling short, originally putting forward, while afrāṭ is excess and tafrīṭ is delay or shortcoming.
rows.anchor: والحسرة شدة الندم حتى يحسر النادم كما يحسر الذي تقوم به دابته في السفر البعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wizr means a burden and is etymologically linked to a cord of reliance; wazīr is likened to someone on whom a ruler relies.
rows.anchor: والوزر الثقل في اللغة واشتقاقه من الوزر وهو الحبل الذي يعتصم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yazirūn is a verb from wizr, “to sin”; mawzūr describes one burdened by wrongdoing, while common speech substitutes maʾzūr. The related Qurʾānic use of wazīr is cited.
rows.anchor: ويزرون يفعلون من وزر يزر وزرا إذا أثم. وقيل: وزر فهو موزور إذا فعل به ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAql, nahy, and ḥijā share the sense of restraint: reason restrains wrongdoing and the self; nahy implies holding back, while ḥijā is from remaining or holding fast.
rows.anchor: والعقل والنهي والحجي متقاربة المعنى فالعقل الإمساك عن القبيح وقصر النفس وحبسها

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī explains that a place called Maʿqala holds water, just as medicine restrains the belly, illustrating the restraining sense of ʿaql.
rows.anchor: الأصمعي: وبالدهناء خبراء يقال له معقلة قال وتراها سميت معقلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nahy can be a verbal noun or a plural and conveys holding and restraint; its related terms name the low place where water stops and collects.
rows.anchor: والنهى لا يخلو أن يكون مصدرا كالهدى أو جمعا كالظلم وهو في معنى ثبات وحبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥijā comes from ḥajw, lingering or holding back; a cited verse witnesses ḥajā, and al-Azharī says taḥajjaytu means I held fast, with or without hamza.
rows.anchor: الحجى أصله من الحجو وهو احتباس وتمكث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “until the Hour comes” marks the endpoint of their denial; the governing verb is “they denied,” and the sudden Hour brings regret too late to help.
rows.anchor: معناها منتهى تكذيبهم الحسرة يوم القيامة والعامل فيها كذبوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling to regret is an emphatic Arabic device: a grave matter is cast as a vocative, summoning regret to appear. Al-Zajjāj and Sībawayh explain it as an attention-getting call whose real addressee is the audience.
rows.anchor: إن العرب إذا اجتهدت في المبالغة في الإخبار عن أمر عظيم تقع فيه جعلته نداء فلفظه لفظ ما ينبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How bad is what they bear” is parsed as “evil is the burden they carry,” applying the previously discussed syntax of niʿma and biʾsa.
rows.anchor: وقوله ساءنا يزرون تقديره بئس الشيء يزرونه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan take meeting God as meeting what God promised of reward and punishment, figuratively attributing the meeting of recompense to God.
rows.anchor: يعني بلقاء ما وعد الله به من الثواب والعقاب وجعل لقائهم لذلك لقاء له تعالى مجازا عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation takes “meeting God” as meeting His recompense, as in saying a dead person has met the reward of his deed.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بلقاء جزاء الله كما يقال للميت لقي فلان عمله أي لقي جزاء عمله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Meeting God means meeting what God promised of reward and punishment; Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan call this a figurative attribution of meeting the recompense to meeting God.
rows.anchor: إلى يوم يلقونه بما أخلفوا الله ما وعدوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes “meeting God” as meeting the recompense of God, as in saying that a dead person has met his deed’s reward.
rows.anchor: أي القيامة { بغتة } أي فجأة من غير أن يعلموا وقتها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The regret is for failing in worldly life to prepare deeds for the Hereafter, according to Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: أي على ما تركنا وضيعنا في الدنيا من تقديم أعمال الآخرة عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes the pronoun in “fīhā” to refer to the Hour: they regret neglecting work and preparation for it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الهاء يعود إلى الساعة عن الحسن

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī takes the pronoun to refer to Paradise: they regret failing to seek and work for it. A report from the Prophet says the people of Hell see their places in Paradise and lament.
rows.anchor: إن الهاء يعود إلى الجنة أي في طلبها والعمل لها عن السدي يدل عليه ما رواه الأعمش

rows.speaker: محمد بن جرير
rows.claim: Muḥammad b. Jarīr says the pronoun refers to the transaction, inferred from the mention of loss; alternatively, it refers to the good deeds neglected, with mā relative rather than a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن جرير: الهاء يعود إلى الصفقة لأنه لما ذكر الخسران

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Carrying burdens on their backs means bearing the weight of their sins and offenses, according to Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: يريد آثامهم وخطاياهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda and al-Suddī describe deeds as embodied companions: good deeds carry believers after resurrection, while evil deeds ride and burden disbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة والسدي: إن المؤمن إذا خرج من قبره استقبله أحسن شيء صورة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj reads the carrying as a permissible metaphor: punishment for sins weighs on them like a heavy load, since weight can describe distress as well as physical mass.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: هذا مثل جائز أن يكون جعل ما ينالهم من العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Evil is what they bear” either condemns the burden itself, as Ibn ʿAbbās says, or the punishment they suffer as recompense for their evil deeds.
rows.anchor: أي بئس الحمل حملهم عن ابن عباس. وقيل: معناه ساء ما ينالهم جزاء لذنوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly life is play and amusement when its works do not lead to the Hereafter; the world itself and God-pleasing deeds are not meant, since play has no lasting benefit and amusement diverts from serious purpose. Alternatively, worldly pleasure simply passes quickly.
rows.anchor: وإنما عنى بالحياة الدنيا أعمال الدنيا لأن نفس الدنيا لا توصف باللعب وما فيه رضا الله من عمل الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hereafter is better for the God-fearing because its bliss lasts; the verse consoles the poor deprived of worldly goods and rebukes the rich who cling to them without preparing for the next life.
rows.anchor: { خير للذين يتقون } معاصي الله لأنها باقية دائمة لا يزول عنهم نعيمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medinan readers and Ibn ʿĀmir through Ibn Dhakwān lighten the nūn in “a-tuḥājjūnī”; the rest double it. The light form deletes the second nūn to avoid doubling, preserving the inflectional first nūn.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل المدينة وابن عامر في رواية ابن ذكوان أتحاجوني خفيفة النون والباقون بالتشديد

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī argues that the second nūn is omitted in the light reading because repetition is heavy; deleting the first would remove inflection, and he cites analogous nūn deletion in speech and poetry.
rows.anchor: فأما وجه التخفيف فإنه حذفت النون الثانية لالتقاء النونين والتضعيف يكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception in “unless my Lord wills something” is parsed as an independent exception meaning Abraham fears only God’s will; an alternative makes it connected, if God empowers the idols to harm or benefit.
rows.anchor: موضع أن يشاء نصب أي لا أخاف إلا مشيئة الله وهذا استثناء منقطع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham says God guided him to know and affirm divine unity; he does not fear idols, since a broken idol cannot defend itself and a setting star is created, so neither can harm or benefit.
rows.anchor: وفقني لمعرفته ولطف بي في العلم بتوحيده وترك الشرك وإخلاص العبادة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of the exception is that if God gave the idols power to harm or benefit, this would itself prove they were created and God alone merits worship; the author calls this the stronger view.
rows.anchor: والأول أجود. ثم احتج ع عليهم وأكد الحجاج بقوله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan instead understands Abraham to fear only that God may punish him for some sin or independently will harm him.
rows.anchor: والثاني: قول الحسن معناه لا أخاف الأوثان إلا أن يشاء ربي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading of Abraham’s question is that he is free of his people’s shirk, so he need not fear that God will punish him for their act of associating partners.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه كيف أخاف شرككم وأنا منه برىء والله تعالى لا يعاقبني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Without authority sent down” means without proof; the verse establishes that anyone advancing a claim or doctrine without evidence is wrong.
rows.anchor: أي حجة على صحته وهذا يدل على أن كل من قال قولا أو اعتقد مذهبا بغير حجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two parties are Abraham and his people: the monotheists who know God through proofs are more entitled to security than those worshipping idols, if they reason without partisan stubbornness.
rows.anchor: أنحن وقد عرفنا الله بأدلته ووجهنا العبادة نحوه أم أنتم وقد أشركتم بعبادة غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, ẓulm is putting something outside its proper place; poetry uses the word for improperly cutting a camel or diverting rain from its course.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي: الظلم في اللغة وضع الشيء في غير موضعه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “Not mixing faith with injustice” means not mixing it with shirk, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib, Qatāda, Mujāhid, and most exegetes hold; Ubay b. Kaʿb cites Luqmān’s declaration that shirk is grave injustice.
rows.anchor: والظلم هو الشرك عن ابن عباس وسعيد بن المسيب وقتادة ومجاهد وأكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports that the verse troubled the Companions, who asked who had not wronged himself; the Prophet clarified that the intended injustice was shirk, citing Luqmān 31:13.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن مسعود قال:

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī and al-Balkhī say injustice includes every grave sin that cancels the reward of obedience, broader than shirk alone.
rows.anchor: وقال الجبائي والبلخي: يدخل في الظلم كل كبيرة تحبط ثواب الطاعة

rows.speaker: البلخي
rows.claim: Al-Balkhī argues that restricting injustice to shirk would imply an unrepentant major sinner is secure, which conflicts with rejection of irjāʾ; the author responds that this inference does not follow from the verse’s implication and other evidence makes such a sinner insecure.
rows.anchor: ولو اختص الشرك على ما قالوه لوجب أن يكون مرتكب الكبيرة إذا كان مؤمنا كان آمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Security is reward and protection from punishment, while being guided means judged to follow truth and religion; another interpretation takes it as guidance to Paradise.
rows.anchor: من الله بحصول الثواب والأمان من العقاب

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: One view, transmitted from ʿAlī, makes the statement part of Abraham’s speech to his people.
rows.anchor: إنه من تمام قول إبراهيم ع وروي ذلك عن علي ع.

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Muḥammad b. Isḥāq, Ibn Zayd, and al-Jubbāʾī instead take it as God’s judgment resolving the dispute between Abraham and his people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن هذا القول من الله تعالى على جهة فصل القضاء بذلك بين إبراهيم ع وقومه عن محمد بن إسحاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʿālaw is an invitation upward even when speaker and hearer are on level ground; tilāwa is recitation distinct from the original recited speech, as narration differs from what it narrates. Imlāq means poverty; fawāḥish are gravely indecent acts.
rows.anchor: تعالوا مشتق من العلو على تقدير أن الداعي في المكان العالي وإن كان في مستو من الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “recite what your Lord forbade” may be a relative clause, the object of forbidding, or an explanatory quotation of what He forbade; “that you associate nothing” can be parsed as an omitted purpose or as an injunction, following al-Zajjāj.
rows.anchor: ما حرم ربكم في موضع نصب بقوله أتل المعنى أتل الذي حرمه ربكم عليكم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj also allows “that you associate nothing” to depend on “I recite to you,” and takes “kindness to parents” as an understood “I enjoin you.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون على معنى أوصيكم أن لا تشركوا به شيئا لأن قوله وبالوالدين إحسانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “associate” may be subjunctive with an as-clause and negative lā, or jussive as a prohibition; in the former parse the later “do not kill” shifts from statement to prohibition, as in 6:14.
rows.anchor: وتشركوا يجوز أن يكون منصوبا بأن ويكون لا للنفي ويجوز أن يكون مجزوما بلا على النهي

rows.speaker: البصير الأصفهاني
rows.claim: Al-Baṣīr al-Aṣfahānī proposes pausing after “upon you,” then beginning “that you associate not”; another possibility treats mā as interrogative and pauses after “your Lord.”
rows.anchor: وقال جامع العلوم البصير الأصفهاني يجوز أن تقف على عليكم ثم تبتدىء بأن لا تشركوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The list of prohibitions follows the account of the polytheists’ invented bans; the Prophet is told to invite them and begin with the prohibition of associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: لما حكى سبحانه عنهم تحريم ما حرموه عقبه بذكر المحرمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not associate anything with Him” and “He forbids that you associate” express the same prohibition, since a command to refrain entails a ban.
rows.anchor: ولا فرق بين أن تقول لا تشركوا به شيئا وبين أن تقول حرم ربكم عليكم أن تشركوا به شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further parsing ends the first clause at “your Lord forbade,” then treats “upon you, that you associate nothing” as an obligation, like the construction in 5:105.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل أيضا إن الكلام قد تم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kindness to parents is enjoined after worship of God because parents’ blessings follow God’s blessings in rank.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت نعم الوالدين تالية نعم الله سبحانه في الرتبة أمر بالإحسان إليهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The ban on killing children from poverty addresses fear of destitution; God provides for both parents and children, according to Ibn ʿAbbās and others.
rows.anchor: أي خوفا من الفقر عن ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: “Do not approach indecencies, open or hidden” covers all sins and wrongs, whether outward or concealed, according to al-Ḥasan.
rows.anchor: أي المعاصي والقبائح كلها { ما ظهر منها وما بطن } أي ظاهرها وباطنها عن الحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddī say people tolerated secret adultery while forbidding it publicly, so both are prohibited; Abū Jaʿfar identifies the apparent act as zina and the hidden one as an illicit intimate relationship.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم كانوا لا يرون بالزنا في السر بأسا ويمنعون منه علانية فنهى الله سبحانه عنه في الحالتين عن ابن عباس والضحاك والسدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan’s alternative takes the apparent as bodily acts and hidden as acts of the heart; the author says this is the broadest and most beneficial interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن ما ظهر أفعال الجوارح وما بطن أفعال القلوب فالمراد ترك المعاصي كلها وهذا أعم فائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Homicide is repeated despite falling under indecencies to emphasize its gravity. The protected life is that of a Muslim or treaty-holder, not a combatant; lawful causes of execution are retaliation, adultery after chastity, and apostasy.
rows.anchor: أعاد ذكر القتل وإن كان داخلا في الفواحش تفخيما لشأنه وتعظيما لأمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing reminder means that God commanded these matters so people would understand, distinguish what He permits from what He forbids, and obey; “He enjoined” is understood in the opening list.
rows.anchor: خطاب لجميع الخلق أي ما ذكر في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports the theological principle that obligation includes refraining from an act, and that one deserves reward or punishment for refraining; this is the author’s school’s position.
rows.anchor: دلالة على أن التكليف قد يتعلق بأن لا يفعل كما يتعلق بالفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kufan readers except Abū Bakr lighten the dhāl in tadhakkarūn; others double it. The light form deletes the first tāʾ from the underlying tatadhakkarūn, while the doubled form assimilates the second tāʾ into dhāl.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل الكوفة إلا أبا بكر تذكرون بتخفيف الذال حيث وقع والباقون بالتشديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers open the hamza in wa-anna hādhā; Kufans other than ʿĀṣim read it with kasra. All double its nūn except Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb, who lighten it; Ibn ʿĀmir opens the yāʾ in ṣirāṭī, and Ibn ʿĀmir and Ibn Kathīr read sirāṭ with sīn, while Ḥamza uses an intermediate sound.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل الكرفة غير عاصم وإن هذا بكسر الهمزة والباقون بفتحها وكلهم شدد النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening wa-anna links the path clause to “follow it,” on a construction like 2:19; with kasra it starts a new sentence. The light form of inna has an understood pronoun of the matter and ṣirāṭī as its predicate.
rows.anchor: وأما من فتح وإن هذا فإنه حملها على فاتبعوه على قياس قول سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light and doubled forms of tadhakkarūn are close in meaning and derive from tatadhakkarūn; the source explains deletion versus assimilation of tāʾ.
rows.anchor: القراءتان في تذكرون متقاربتان والأصل تتذكرون فمن خفف حذف التاء الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashudd can be a singular or plural, meaning the firm strength of youth and age; some derive it from shidda, while one Basran account treats it as a singular like al-ānuk. Dhikr and dhakar share a meaning; doubling the verb makes it take two objects.
rows.anchor: الأشد واحدها شد مثل الأشر في جمع شر والأضر في جمع ضر والشد القوة وهو استحكام قوة الشباب

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh says the noun dhikr and dhakar have the same meaning; the verse’s doubled verb is causative, and tadhakkara is the reflexive counterpart, as a poetic example illustrates.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه الذكر والذكر بمعنى وذكر فعل يتعدى إلى مفعول واحد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddī say the guardian may develop the orphan’s property through trade.
rows.anchor: إلا بتثمير ماله بالتجارة عن مجاهد والضحاك والسدي

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and al-Jubbāʾī permit the guardian to take customary food from the orphan’s property, but not clothing.
rows.anchor: بأن يأخذ القيم عليه بالأكل بالمعروف دون الكسوة عن ابن زيد والجبائي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says to preserve the orphan’s property until the child grows up.
rows.anchor: وثالثها: بأن يحفظ عليه حتى يكبر

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: The orphan reaches ashudd at puberty, according to al-Shaʿbī; another view sets it at eighteen, while al-Suddī says thirty and considers that limit abrogated by 4:6.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو أن يبلغ ثماني عشرة سنة وقال السدي: هو أن يبلغ ثلاثين سنة ثم نسخها قوله

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa says the property is given to the orphan at twenty-five; before then, it is withheld if sound judgment has not been established.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة: إذا بلغ خمسا وعشرين سنة دفع المال إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest view sets no fixed age: the person must reach adulthood, mature mentally, and show sound judgment. Maturity itself does not permit inferior use; then the guardian must hand over the property, as 4:6 clarifies.
rows.anchor: وهذا أقوى الوجوه وليس بلوغ اليتيم أشده مما يبيح قرب ماله بغير الأحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fair fulfillment of measures and weights means avoiding short measure and short weight. Since exact precision at the smallest degree is difficult, one must diligently guard against deficiency to the extent possible.
rows.anchor: بالعدل والوفاء من غير بخس { لا نكلف نفسا إلا وسعها } أي إلا ما يسعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Speak justly even about a relative” means tell the truth; making justice habitual in speech also draws one toward just action. Another interpretation specifically covers testimony and judgment concerning relatives and encompasses legal statements and rulings.
rows.anchor: وإنما خص القول بالعدل دون الفعل لأن من جعل عادته العدل في القول دعاه ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s covenant can mean every obligation God imposed through command and proof, or lawful vows and agreements that people made with God; both require fulfillment.
rows.anchor: قيل في معنى عهد الله قولان أحدهما: أن كل ما أوجبه الله تعالى على العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing exhortation means remember God’s instructions and act on them rather than neglect them; “enjoined” gathers up the orphan-property, measures, fairness, and covenant commands.
rows.anchor: أي لكي تتذكروه وتأخذوا به فلا تطرحوه ولا تغفلوا عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains “this is My straight path” as the religion of Abrahamic monotheism, the upright and best religion; the listed commands lead to reward and Paradise.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد أن هذا ديني دين الحنيفية أقوم الأديان وأحسنها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the forbidden divergent paths as disbelief, innovations, and doubtful doctrines.
rows.anchor: ولا تتبعوا السبل } أي طرق الكفر والبدع والشبهات عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following divergent paths scatters people away from the religion God chose and enjoined.
rows.anchor: أي فتشتت وتميل وتخالف بكم عن دينه الذي ارتضى وبه أوصى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the divergent paths as Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and idol worship; they divert people from God’s chosen religion.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يريد اليهودية والنصرانية والمجوسية وعبادة الأوثان عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb fattafarraqa is originally fatatafarraqa; following divergent ways scatters people away from God’s path, the religion He chose and enjoined, and the commands are meant to guard against His punishment.
rows.anchor: وأصله فتتفرق { بكم عن سبيله } أي فتشتت وتميل وتخالف بكم عن دينه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls these rulings clear, un-abrogated prohibitions in all scriptures and universal commands for humanity: those who act on them enter Paradise and those who abandon them enter Hell.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هذه الآيات محكمات لم ينسخهن شيء من جميع الكتب

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār swears that these commands are the Torah’s first instruction, beginning with “Say: come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden.”
rows.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار: والذي نفس كعب بيده إن هذا لأول شيء في التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ reads “a-amantum” with one hamza as a declaration; the rest use two hamzas as a question. The readings both rebuke the magicians, and the second hamza may be fully articulated or softened between hamza and alif.
rows.anchor: قرأ حفص عن عاصم آمنتم بهمزة واحدة على الخبر حيث كان والباقون بهمزتين على الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh accuses the magicians of conspiring with Moses in the city to drive out its people; he aims to deceive the crowd into thinking their belief is a political plot rather than recognition of truth.
rows.anchor: أراد فرعون بهذا القول التلبيس على الناس وإيهامهم أن إيمان السحرة لم يكن عن علم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative says the magicians arranged the plan with Moses in Egypt before coming, intending to take over Egypt and expel its people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه إن هذا لصنيع صنعتموه فيما بينكم وبين موسى في مصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s threat to cut hands and feet crosswise means taking opposite-side limbs; al-Ḥasan specifies right hand with left foot or left hand with right foot.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: هو أن يقطع اليد اليمنى مع الرجل اليسرى وكذلك اليد اليسرى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A report says Pharaoh was the first to amputate and crucify, fastening them to date-palm trunks along the Nile in Egypt.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن أول من قطع الرجل وصلب فرعون صلبهم في جذوع النخل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The magicians say they will return to God with monotheism and sincerity; their return is to His recompense, and remembering reward steadies them while they answer Pharaoh’s threat with confidence in God’s harsher punishment.
rows.anchor: أي راجعون إلى ربنا بالتوحيد والإخلاص عن ابن عباس والانقلاب إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: They say Pharaoh finds nothing to punish except their faith in God’s signs that Moses brought, which they recognized as from God and beyond anyone but Him to produce.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: معناه ما لنا عندك من ذنب ولا ركبنا منك مكروها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Crucifixion derives from fastening someone to wood and all Qurʾānic readers double its lām; na-qima can mean punish or object, while “punishment” contrasts with a blameworthy injury. Ifrāgh is pouring out, and ṣabr is restraining visible despair; patience for truth is honor.
rows.anchor: الصلب الشد على الخشبة وغيرها وأصله من صلابة الشيء والقراء كلهم على تشديد اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prayer asks God to pour patience over them during amputation and crucifixion: aid them to endure bravely without fear or apostasy.
rows.anchor: أي أصبب علينا الصبر عند القطع والصلب حتى لا نرجع كفارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Take us as Muslims” means keep them steadfast in faith until death; another interpretation asks to remain sincerely devoted so persecution will not turn them from their religion.
rows.anchor: أي وفقنا للثبات على الإيمان والإسلام إلى وقت الوفاة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One account says Pharaoh crucified them that very day, making them martyrs after they had been magicians that morning; another says he never reached them because God protected them.
rows.anchor: قالوا فصلبهم فرعون من يومه فكانوا أول النهار كفارا سحرة وآخر النهار شهداء بررة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Insilākh is emerging from what enclosed something, by analogy with skinning a sheep; ḥaṣr is confinement, and marṣad is a path or lookout where someone is watched.
rows.anchor: الانسلاخ خروج الشيء مما لابسه وأصله من سلخ الشاة وهو نزع الجلد عنها

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash takes “every marṣad” to mean “at every marṣad,” with the preposition omitted, and cites a line that means “we charge a high price for meat” with an omitted bi-.
rows.anchor: الأخفش: قوله { كل مرصد } المعنى على كل مرصد فحذفت على أنشد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses “every marṣad” as an adverbial place noun, like a destination in “I went a way.”
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: كل مرصد ظرف كقولك ذهبت مذهبا وذهبت طريقا

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says no preposition is needed if marṣad names a place, but if it means a particular road the verb ordinarily needs one; he rejects al-Zajjāj’s treatment of a road as an adverbial place noun, citing Sībawayh and poetry for occasional omission.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: لا يحتاج في هذا إلى تقدير على إذا كان المرصد اسما للمكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “if anyone of the polytheists seeks your protection,” a hidden verb raises “one”; it means “if anyone seeks refuge with you.” Al-Zajjāj rejects raising it as a subject because a conditional clause’s governing verb cannot skip it.
rows.anchor: وقوله: { أحد } فإعرابه أنه مرفوع بفعل مضمر الذي ظهر تفسيره

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī counters that a jussive verb may follow a conditional subject; the usual conditional answer has an underlying verb, and Sībawayh permits the construction criticized by al-Zajjāj.
rows.anchor: ولكن لا يمتنع أن يقع الجزم بعد الفاعل في الجزاء كما يقع في الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “sacred months” may be the familiar Dhū al-Qaʿda, Dhū al-Ḥijja, Muḥarram, and Rajab, or the four months of safe passage granted to the polytheists; each reading yields different dates for the end of the truce.
rows.anchor: قيل: هي الأشهر الحرم المعروفة ذو القعدة وذو الحجة والمحرم ورجب ثلاثة سرد وواحد فرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one chronology, the four-month respite began with the revelation of Barāʾa in Shawwāl for treaty-holders, while others were given until the end of the sacred months after the proclamation at ʿArafa or the Sacrifice; another chronology counts twenty days of Dhū al-Ḥijja, Muḥarram, Ṣafar, Rabīʿ I, and ten days of Rabīʿ II.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال: معناه { إذا انسلخ الأشهر } الأربعة التي هي عشرون من ذي الحجة والمحرم وصفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the period, the command to fight applies wherever polytheists are found, in or out of the sanctuary, and abrogates earlier verses directing peace or turning away.
rows.anchor: أي فضعوا السيف فيهم حيث كانوا في الأشهر الحرم وغيرها في الحل أو في الحرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Take them” may be moved conceptually before “kill them,” or the commands may offer alternatives chosen according to what is expedient; confinement can mean imprisonment, enslavement, ransom, or barring them from Mecca and Muslim territory.
rows.anchor: قيل: فيه تقديم وتأخير وتقديره فخذوا المشركين حيث وجدتموهم واقتلوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lying in ambush means watching every road and place they might pass, to make capture or killing possible.
rows.anchor: أي بكل طريق وبكل مكان تظنون أنهم يمرون فيه وضيقوا المسالك عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance, acceptance of prayer, and acceptance of almsgiving restore their protected status; actual performance of prayer and zakat is not a condition for blood immunity.
rows.anchor: لأن عصمة الدم لا تقف على إقامة الصلاة وأداء الزكاة فثبت أن المراد به القبول

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation releases them to go to the House and perform pilgrimage with the Muslims.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه فخلوا سبيلهم إلى البيت أي دعوهم يحجوا معكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional wording is used to argue that someone who deliberately abandons prayer must be killed, because killing is forbidden if they repent and establish prayer; the author reports this inference.
rows.anchor: واستدلوا بهذه الآية على أن من ترك الصلاة متعمدا يجب قتله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A polytheist may seek protection after the four months to hear the Qurʾān and its proofs; grant safety and time to understand it, then escort him to his secure homeland if he does not convert, lest protection become betrayal.
rows.anchor: معناه وإن طلب أحد من المشركين الذين أمرتك بقتالهم منك الأمان من القتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says “God’s speech” because the Qurʾān contains the main body of the proofs; those people are ignorant of faith and its evidence, so they should hear and consider it. This rebuts the claim that religious knowledge is innate and necessary.
rows.anchor: وإنما خص كلام الله لأن معظم الأدلة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recited and heard Qurʾān is itself God’s speech: ordinary Arabic and legal convention call an author’s words “the speech” or “poetry” of that author, despite recitation.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دلالة على أن المتلو والمسموع كلام الله لأن الشرع والعرب جعلا الحكاية كعين المحكي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medinan readers and Ibn ʿĀmir read “words” in the plural here, at the end of the sūra, and in Sūrat al-Muʾmin; the rest read the singular “word.”
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل المدينة وابن عامر كلمات ههنا وفي آخرها على الجمع وكذلك في سورة المؤمن والباقون على التوحيد

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The singular may call the entire promised punishment one “word,” as a whole poem or sermon is called a word, or use the generic singular for part of a class, as in the cited Qurʾānic wording and poetry.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي من قرأ على التوحيد احتمل وجهين أحدهما: أن يكون جعل ما أوعد به الفاسقون كلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The increasing punishment may mean a further punishment above the first, as also stated at 16:88; or successive punishments equal to or greater than the last, endlessly, in proportion to desert; or special doubling for leaders who misled followers, adding the punishment of leading others astray.
rows.anchor: وثانيها: أن معناه أنه كلما مضى ضرب من العذاب يعقبه ضرب آخر

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Balkhī explain that they could hear and see but deliberately refused the truth; the preposition bi- is understood though omitted, as in cited poetry.
rows.anchor: يستطيعون السمع فلا يسمعون وبما كانوا يستطيعون الإبصار فلا يبصرون عنادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says their aversion to hearing God’s signs made them as though unable to hear, while their eyes were useless because they would not reflect; al-Aʿshā’s rhetorical question similarly denies an ability that the speaker in fact has.
rows.anchor: لاستثقالهم استماع آيات الله وكراهتهم تذكرها وتفهمها جروا مجرى من لا يستطيع السمع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās offers the more remote view that the pronouns refer to idols: they could not hear or see.
rows.anchor: وروي ذلك عن ابن عباس وفيه أدنى بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further grammatical reading takes mā as temporal rather than negative: their punishment lasts as long as they live, like the expression “I will remain as long as a star appears.”
rows.anchor: أن ما هنا ليست للنفي بل تجري مجرى قولهم لأواصلنك ما لاح نجم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They lose themselves by doing what earns punishment and destruction; loss of one’s self is the greatest loss because it has no replacement, and their fabricated gods and claims disappear.
rows.anchor: من حيث فعلوا ما استحقوا به العقاب فهلكوا فذلك خسران أنفسهم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses lā jarama as denying what they thought would benefit them, so their conduct earns the greatest loss; another explanation takes the expression as “necessarily” or “surely,” a decisive assertion that they are the greatest losers in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: لا نفي لما ظنوا أنه ينفعهم كأن المعنى لا ينفعهم ذلك جرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account links the proof-bearing verse to the challenge to produce ten comparable sūras: if they fail, ask whether someone with clear proof is like one without proof.
rows.anchor: اتصلت الآية الأولى بقوله { قل فأتوا بعشر سور } مثله والمراد أنهم إذا لم يأتوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account connects the passage to the one who desires worldly life, contrasting striving in religion with making worldly life the sole aim.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اتصلت بقوله { من كان يريد الحياة الدنيا } أي من كان مجتهدا في الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clarification about the unjust forger answers people who thought ignorance of God would not harm them: one who does not know God may also lie about Him, and none is more unjust than such a liar.
rows.anchor: أنه سبحانه أراد أن يبين حال العاقل والغافل فكأنهم قالوا وما يضرنا أن لا نعرف ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza in dhiʾb may be softened; al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf, Abū Jaʿfar, Warsh, al-Aʿshā, and al-Yazīdī soften it in all three occurrences, while the rest articulate it. Plurals include adhuʾub, dhawāʾib, and dhuʾbān; tadhāʾabat the wind means it blew from every direction.
rows.anchor: وقراءة الكسائي وخلف وأبو جعفر وورش والأعشى واليزيدي بتخفيف الهمزة في المواضع الثلاث والباقون بالهمز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥuzn and aḥzan are both used for sorrow; shuʿūr is subtle perception, and ʿishāʾ may mean the late day, early night, or the period of the evening prayer.
rows.anchor: الشعور إدراك الشيء بمثل الشعرة في الدقة ومنه المشاعر في البدن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istibāq means racing to find who is fastest; archery contests are permitted by consensus, horse and camel races are permitted by the author’s school, while foot races for prizes are barred by that school and al-Shāfiʿī but allowed by Abū Ḥanīfa and some of the author’s colleagues; the same dispute applies to wrestling.
rows.anchor: والاستباق افتعال من السبق واستبقا تبادرا حتى يظهر الأقوى ومنه المسابقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase dam kadhib may mean blood falsely attributed to Joseph, or be parsed as a verbal noun meaning “falsified”; al-Farrāʾ accepts a verbal noun for the passive sense, but Sībawayh rejects that analysis and offers an alternative ellipsis. ʿĀʾisha’s reading kadb with dāl means fresh blood.
rows.anchor: ودم كذب أي مكذوب فيه وهو مصدر وصف به. وقيل: إن تقديره بدم ذي كذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to “if the wolf eats him” is omitted after the oath: “when they took him away” means the plot they intended was grave. Kūfan grammarians treat the wāw in “and they agreed” as inserted, but Basrans reject that without proof and analyze the syntax otherwise.
rows.anchor: هي اللام التي يتلقى بها القسم { وإنا إذا لخاسرون } جواب القسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kūfans cite poetry for an inserted wāw in ajmaʿū; Basrans say the examples have an omitted answer, rejecting insertion as lacking evidence or analogy.
rows.anchor: والكوفيون يقولون: الواو في وأجمعوا مقحمة وتقديره أجمعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s crying is parsed circumstantially, ʿishāʾ as a time adverb, and “we were racing” as another circumstantial clause; “while they did not realize” may modify either the later promise or the revelation.
rows.anchor: وقوله { يبكون } في موضع نصب على الحال وعشاء منصوب على الظرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Beautiful patience” may predicate an omitted “my affair” or “my patience,” or be a subject with an omitted predicate; a non-Qurʾānic accusative is also reported as an exhortation to the self, with poetic parallels.
rows.anchor: وصبر جميل مرفوع على أحد وجهين على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف وتقديره فشأني صبر جميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob says Yusuf’s departure grieves him and he fears a wolf will eat him in the desert while his brothers are distracted; the fear clause describes their being inattentive. The land was said to be full of fierce wolves.
rows.anchor: أي يغمني { أن تذهبوا به } وتغيبوه عني

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Jacob feared the separation itself; some say a dream showed ten wolves attacking Yusuf, one protecting him, and Yusuf entering the earth for three days, which prompted the warning.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه يحزنني مفارقته إياي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic report says not to supply someone with a lie: Jacob’s hint taught the brothers that a wolf might eat a human. The author draws a general lesson against furnishing an opponent with an argument.
rows.anchor: لا تلقنوا الكذب فيكذبوا فإن بني يعقوب لم يعلموا أن الذئب يأكل الإنسان حتى لقنهم أبوهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Jacob feared that his sons would kill Joseph and alluded to them as wolves to accommodate their feelings.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه خاف عليه أن يقتلوه فكنى عنهم بالذئب مسايرة لهم قال ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers claim that, as a mutually supportive group, they would be losers if a wolf ate Yusuf under their watch; “losers” may mean ruined, helpless, or heedless in a Qays dialect. Al-Ḥasan says they feared for him more than they feared a wolf.
rows.anchor: أي جماعة متعاضدون متناصرون نرى الذئب قد قصده ولا نمنعه منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanation for sending him is omitted: Jacob agreed to meet their request so it could produce familiarity and affection.
rows.anchor: وههنا حذف والتقدير أنه أرسله معهم إجابة لما سألوه ليؤدي ذلك إلى الإلفة والمحبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They unanimously resolved to hide Yusuf in the well’s deep recess; “agreed” implies all their motives converged, and the definite article suggests a familiar well frequented by travelers.
rows.anchor: أي عزموا جميعا { أن يجعلوه في غيابة الجب } أي قعر البئر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say they chose a well with little water, deep enough to conceal him but not drown him; another view places him at its side.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم طلبوا بئرا قليلة الماء تغيبه ولا تغرقه فجعلوه فيها.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One narrative says they first treated him as beloved, then beat him in the open country; as they prepared to kill him, Judah stopped them.
rows.anchor: فلما وصلوا إلى الصحراء أظهروا له العداوة وجعلوا يضربونه وهو يستغيث بواحد

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the brothers stripped Joseph’s shirt, lowered him by a rope, dropped him into the well, and left him on a rock; Judah brought him food.
rows.anchor: فدلوه في البئر حتى إذا بلغ نصفها ألقوه إرادة أن يموت وكان في البئر ماء فسقط فيه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other reports say the well brightened and its water became sweet, sustaining Joseph without food; Muqātil says cloudy water cleared, an angel guarded and fed him, and another says Gabriel comforted him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الجب أضاء له وعذب ماؤه حتى أغناه عن الطعام والشراب.

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil reports that God cleared the well’s muddy water and appointed an angel to guard and feed Joseph.
rows.anchor: وكل الله به ملكا يحرسه ويطعمه عن مقاتل.

rows.speaker: مفضل بن عمر
rows.claim: A report from al-Mufaḍḍal b. ʿUmar, from al-Ṣādiq, says Gabriel raised a rock, clothed naked Joseph in the Paradise shirt inherited through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and explains the shirt Jacob later recognized by scent.
rows.anchor: وروى ذلك مفضل بن عمر عن الصادق ع قال وهو القميص الذي وجد يعقوب ريحه

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: In a report in Kitāb al-Nubuwwa, al-Ṣādiq recounts Gabriel asking Joseph who put him in the well; Joseph names his brothers and says they envied his place with their father.
rows.anchor: وفي كتاب النبوة عن الحسن بن محبوب عن الحسن بن عمارة عن مسمع أبي سيار عن الصادق ع قال لما ألقى إخوة يوسف يوسف في الجب

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: The report has Gabriel teach Joseph a supplication asking God for relief, deliverance, and provision; God gives him an exit from the well and a path out of a woman’s plot, then grants him Egypt’s rule unexpectedly.
rows.anchor: فإن إله إبراهيم وإسحاق ويعقوب يقول لك قل اللهم إني أسألك بأن لك الحمد لا إله إلا أنت

rows.speaker: علي بن إبراهيم
rows.claim: ʿAlī b. Ibrāhīm transmits Joseph’s plea in the well: “God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, have mercy on my weakness, helplessness, and youth.”
rows.anchor: وروى علي بن إبراهيم أن يوسف ع قال في الجب: يا إله إبراهيم وإسحاق ويعقوب ارحم ضعفي

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says God gave Joseph prophethood in the well along with the glad tidings of rescue and kingship.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن أعطاه الله النبوة وهو في الجب والبشارة بالنجاة والملك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda say Joseph received revelation and prophethood in the well, with instructions to conceal his identity, be patient, and later tell his brothers what they had done when they would not recognize him.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وقتادة أوحى الله إليه ونبأه وهو في الجب وكان فيما أوحى إليه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation says the brothers did not realize revelation had come to Joseph; another takes “you will surely tell them” as a threat to repay them for their deed, as in an Arabic idiom.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يريد وهم لا يشعرون بأنه أوحي إليه.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Joseph later recognized his brothers in Egypt, made the cup speak, and disclosed that it revealed they had a paternal brother whom they threw into a well and sold cheaply.
rows.anchor: وقيل أراد بذلك أنهم لما دخلوا مصر عرفهم يوسف وهم له منكرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers returned to Jacob at night or late afternoon to mislead him and make excuses more boldly; their tears were feigned to seem truthful, showing that crying does not prove a claim.
rows.anchor: أي ليلا أو في آخر النهار ليلبسوا على أبيهم وليكونوا أجرأ على الاعتذار

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī and al-Suddī explain “we went racing” as running on foot to see who was fastest; al-Zajjāj takes it to mean target practice, and a reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh is “we were shooting.”
rows.anchor: أي نشتد ونعدو على الأقدام لننظر أينا أعدى وأسبق لصاحبه عن الجبائي والسدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They left Joseph by their baggage to guard it. “You would not believe us even if we were truthful” has an omitted result: Jacob would still disbelieve them because he suspected their jealousy and knew their resentment.
rows.anchor: أي تركناه عند الرحل ليحفظه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid say the brothers killed a young sheep and smeared Joseph’s shirt with its blood; another account says it was a deer. They failed to notice that a wolf would tear the shirt.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم ذبحوا سخلة وجعلوا دمها على قميصه عن ابن عباس ومجاهد. وقيل: ظبيا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Jacob asked to see the intact shirt and remarked that he had never known such a gentle wolf, which ate his son without tearing the garment; another report has him cover his face and call it a merciful wolf.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن وروي أنه ألقى ثوبه على وجهه وقال يا يوسف لقد أكلك ذئب رحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dam kadhib means blood falsely attributed or falsified, like “poured water” meaning water that was poured out.
rows.anchor: مكذوب عليه أوفيه كما يقال ماء سكب أي مسكوب وشراب صب أي مصبوب
